In Daniel Michael fights the princes of Persia and Greece, while in Revelation he fights the dragon himself. Daniel places Michael's rising at a time of great trouble before the resurrection; Revelation links his victory to the child being caught up to God, and the voice from heaven credits the believers' victory to the Lamb's blood rather than to Michael. Luke and John speak of Satan's fall in connection with Jesus' ministry and cross, which many read as the same event Revelation pictures.

Preterists, idealists and many amillennial readers place the war in heaven at Christ's death, resurrection and ascension, which follow the child being caught up. Futurists often place it in the middle of a future seven-year tribulation, when Satan is cast to earth for the last three and a half years. Historicists have linked it to events such as the fall of Roman paganism under Constantine, and Seventh-day Adventists identify Michael with Christ himself.
Locusts from the abyss
The locust plague of Egypt and Joel's invading army return as demonic locusts with a king called Destroyer.
In the eighth plague locusts cover the land of Egypt so that it is darkened and nothing green is left.
Swarm after swarm devours the land, a nation with teeth like a lion's teeth.
The locust army looks like horses, sounds like chariots, darkens sun and moon, and is the LORD's army on his day.
Amos sees God forming locusts to devour the late crop, and pleads for Jacob.
Nineveh's merchants and officials are like locusts that strip the land and fly away.
At the fifth trumpet the shaft of the abyss is opened, smoke darkens the sun, and locusts come out to torment for five months those without God's seal.
The locusts look like horses ready for battle, with human faces, women's hair and lions' teeth, and their king is the angel of the abyss, Abaddon in Hebrew and Apollyon in Greek.

Locusts were the most feared natural disaster in the ancient world, and the prophets used them for God's judgment and for invading armies. Revelation's locusts come from the abyss rather than the fields, do not harm vegetation but people, and torment without killing, which makes them a spiritual or demonic plague. Their king's name, Destroyer, shows what the power behind them really is.

Assyrian and Mesopotamian texts compare invading armies to locust swarms, and locust plagues are recorded throughout the region. Abaddon, 'destruction', is a Hebrew poetic name for the realm of the dead (Job 26:6, 28:22, Psalm 88:11). Many scholars note that the Greek Apollyon resembles the name of the god Apollo, whose symbols in some traditions included the locust, and that emperors such as Nero and, on some accounts, Domitian were associated with Apollo, so the title may hint that the empire's patron god is really the destroyer; this is a suggestion, not a certainty. Five months roughly matches the life cycle or season of the locust, and the long hair has reminded some interpreters of Parthian horsemen.

Egypt's locusts strip the land, while Revelation's are forbidden to harm grass or trees and attack only people without God's seal, echoing Israel's protection in Goshen. Joel's locusts are like horses and armies; Revelation intensifies the comparison with human faces, crowns, iron breastplates and scorpion tails. In Joel the army is the LORD's; in Revelation the locusts have their own destructive king, yet they act only within limits God sets.

Historicists traditionally read the fifth trumpet as the Arab or Saracen invasions of the seventh century, often counting the five months as 150 years. Futurists usually take the locusts as demonic beings released in a future tribulation, while some have suggested modern military aircraft; preterists link them to the demonic and social torment of the Jewish War before AD 70. Idealists see the self-destructive torment that evil and deception bring to those who belong to it.
The Euphrates and the kings from the east
The river that bounded Eden, the promised land and the Roman world is dried up to open the way for kings from the east.
The Euphrates is the fourth of the rivers flowing out of Eden.
God promises Abram's offspring the land from the river of Egypt to the great river, the Euphrates.
The LORD will wave his hand over the River and split it into seven channels, so that people can cross in sandals.
God says to the deep, 'Be dry; I will dry up your rivers', in the verse before he names Cyrus.
A drought will come upon Babylon's waters and they will be dried up, for it is a land of idols.
The LORD will dry up Babylon's sea and make her fountain dry.
At the sixth trumpet four angels bound at the great river Euphrates are released, with a vast cavalry.
The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates to prepare the way for the kings from the east.

The Euphrates marked the edge of the promised land and the gateway from which invading empires such as Assyria and Babylon came. Drying up a river recalls the exodus and the fall of Babylon, so the image signals that God is removing a barrier for his purposes. In Revelation the opened river releases hostile forces gathered for the final battle, and it is also the river of Babylon, whose fall follows in chapters 16 to 18.

Herodotus (1.191) and Xenophon tell how Cyrus took Babylon by diverting the Euphrates and marching in along the riverbed, a story that fits Isaiah's and Jeremiah's drying of Babylon's waters, though the Babylonian Nabonidus Chronicle simply says the city fell without battle. In John's day the Euphrates was roughly Rome's eastern frontier, beyond which lay the Parthians, mounted archers who had defeated Crassus at Carrhae in 53 BC and forced a Roman army to surrender in AD 62. 1 Enoch 56:5-7 pictures angels stirring up the Parthians and Medes against the land, and the Sibylline Oracles (4 and 5) expected Nero to return from beyond the Euphrates with eastern armies.

In Isaiah the River is split so God's exiles can return; in Revelation it is dried so hostile kings can advance, which reverses the exodus pattern. Jeremiah's drying of the waters is judgment on Babylon, and Revelation keeps that link by placing the sixth bowl immediately before Babylon's fall. Revelation 9:14 and 16:12 both centre on the river, with a release of forces at the sixth trumpet and the sixth bowl.

Historicists traditionally read the sixth trumpet as the Turkish invasions and the drying of the Euphrates as the decline of the Ottoman Empire, opening the way for events in the east. Futurists usually expect literal armies from Asia gathering for Armageddon, while preterists point to Roman legions drawn from the Euphrates region for the war against Jerusalem, or to fears of a Parthian invasion of Rome. Idealists read the river as the boundary holding back chaos, whose removal lets evil gather for its own defeat.
Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified
The great city where the witnesses lie is called by the names of the Bible's archetypal places of wickedness and oppression.
The LORD rains sulphur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah and overthrows the cities of the plain.
Egypt sets taskmasters over Israel and makes their lives bitter with hard labour.
Isaiah addresses Jerusalem's rulers and people as rulers of Sodom and people of Gomorrah.
Jerusalem is told she is worse than her sister Sodom, whose guilt was pride, excess and neglect of the poor.
Jesus says it will be more bearable for Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for a town that rejects his messengers.
The witnesses' bodies lie in the street of the great city that is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where also their Lord was crucified.

Sodom stands for arrogance, violence and contempt for the vulnerable, and Egypt for oppression and slavery of God's people. The prophets already used Sodom as a name for faithless Jerusalem, so the label is a prophetic charge rather than a map reference. Revelation says the city is so called 'spiritually' or prophetically, and adds that it is the place where the Lord was crucified, so the city that kills the witnesses repeats the world's rejection of Christ.

Sodom's destruction became a byword for divine judgment across Jewish literature, as in Jubilees 16 and 3 Maccabees 2:5. The Wisdom of Solomon 19:13-17 compares the Egyptians to the people of Sodom for their hostility to strangers, so joining the two names had precedent. Roman Asia's readers knew Egypt as a Roman province and grain supplier, but in Jewish memory it remained the house of bondage.

Isaiah and Ezekiel call Jerusalem Sodom to shame her; Revelation adds Egypt and the crucifixion, making the charge sharper. Matthew compares towns that reject the apostles unfavourably with Sodom, and Revelation likewise places the witnesses' rejection alongside Jesus' own. In Genesis Sodom is destroyed by fire from heaven, while in Revelation 11:13 an earthquake strikes the city and the survivors give glory to God, a more hopeful outcome.

Preterists and many futurists take 'where their Lord was crucified' as pointing to Jerusalem, the first in its first-century state and the second in a future tribulation. Many idealists and some historicists note that 'the great city' elsewhere in Revelation is Babylon (16:19, 17:18) and read it as the world city opposed to God, including Rome, and some older historicists applied it to a particular nation such as Revolutionary France.
Hidden manna and the white stone
The bread from heaven kept before the ark and a white stone bearing a secret new name are promised to the faithful in Pergamum.
In the wilderness a fine, flaky substance covers the ground, and Moses tells Israel it is the bread the LORD has given them.
An omer of manna is placed in a jar before the testimony to be kept for future generations.
God rained down manna for them to eat and gave them the grain of heaven.
After the crowd recalls the manna, Jesus says that he himself is the true bread from heaven, the bread of life.
The ark of the covenant held the golden jar of manna, Aaron's staff and the tablets.
To the one who conquers in Pergamum Christ will give some of the hidden manna and a white stone with a new name that no one knows except the one who receives it.

Manna was God's daily provision in the wilderness, and the jar kept before the ark made it a lasting sign of his care. The 'hidden' manna points to heavenly food kept for the faithful, which John's Gospel identifies with Jesus himself. The white stone with a new name suggests acceptance, admission and a personal, intimate identity given by Christ, set against the idol feasts that tempted the church in Pergamum.

Jewish tradition held that Jeremiah hid the ark and its contents before Jerusalem fell (2 Maccabees 2:4-8), and 2 Baruch 29:8 expects the treasury of manna to come down again from on high in the messianic age. In the Greco-Roman world small stones or tokens (tesserae) served as tickets for admission to feasts and public events, jurors voted for acquittal with white pebbles, and stones inscribed with secret names served as amulets. Pergamum was a centre of pagan cult, including the altar of Zeus, the healing shrine of Asclepius and an early temple of Augustus and Rome, where banquets in honour of gods were part of civic and guild life.

The manna of Exodus was gathered openly every morning; Revelation's is hidden and given only to those who conquer. John 6 speaks of the bread of life now, while Revelation presents the manna as a future reward that answers the refusal of idol food in 2:14. The new name echoes Isaiah 62:2 and 65:15, where God's people receive a new name, but Revelation makes it known only to the one who receives it.

Interpreters of all schools agree that the promise is a reward for faithfulness in Pergamum, though they differ on the white stone's background, whether acquittal, admission token or amulet. Futurists often connect it with the marriage supper of the Lamb and the coming kingdom, preterists and idealists with communion with Christ now and fully at the end, and Spiritual Understanding readers with Christ as the inner bread and a new identity known only in the heart. Some historicist and dispensational readers also see Pergamum as a picture of the church in the age of Constantine.
Balaam, Jezebel and the Nicolaitans
Two Old Testament figures who led Israel into idolatry become code names for teachers urging compromise in Pergamum and Thyatira.
Israel, having escaped Balaam's curses, joins in the sacrificial feasts of Moab and yokes itself to the Baal of Peor.
Moses says the Midianite women acted on Balaam's advice to make Israel act faithlessly at Peor.
Ahab marries Jezebel, daughter of the Sidonian king, and serves Baal; 21:25 says she urged him on in evil.
Jehu tells Joram there can be no peace while the whorings and sorceries of his mother Jezebel continue.
False teachers have gone astray, following the way of Balaam son of Bosor, who loved gain from wrongdoing.
The intruders have abandoned themselves to Balaam's error for the sake of gain.
Christ praises the Ephesian church for hating the works of the Nicolaitans, which he also hates.
Some in Pergamum hold the teaching of Balaam, who put a stumbling block before Israel to eat food sacrificed to idols and commit sexual immorality, and some hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.
Thyatira tolerates 'that woman Jezebel', a self-styled prophetess who leads believers into immorality and idol food, and who is given time to repent.

Balaam, hired by Balak of Moab (Numbers 22:5), could not curse Israel but helped draw it into idolatry, and Jezebel brought Baal worship into Israel's royal house. Revelation uses their names for teachers within the churches who encouraged eating idol food and sexual immorality, which may be literal, or the prophets' figure for unfaithfulness to God, or both. The concern is compromise from inside the church, which Christ treats as more dangerous than persecution from outside.

Thyatira had many trade guilds, known from inscriptions, including wool workers, dyers, leather workers, potters and bronze smiths, and Lydia the purple seller came from there (Acts 16:14). Guild membership often involved banquets in honour of patron gods, where meat sacrificed to idols was served, so refusing could cost a person work and standing; Pergamum likewise had temples of Zeus, Asclepius and the emperor. Paul addresses similar questions about idol food in 1 Corinthians 8-10, and the Jerusalem council forbade it (Acts 15:29). Irenaeus linked the Nicolaitans to Nicolaus of Antioch (Acts 6:5), though this is uncertain, and some scholars suggest that Nicolaitan ('conquer the people') is a Greek play on a Hebrew reading of Balaam as 'consumer of the people'.

Numbers presents Balaam as a foreign seer, while 2 Peter, Jude and Revelation make him a type of the false teacher motivated by gain or compromise. Jezebel in Kings is a queen who persecutes prophets; in Revelation she is a prophetess inside the church, and she is given time to repent, which the original Jezebel was not. Ephesus is praised for rejecting the Nicolaitans, while Pergamum and Thyatira are rebuked for tolerating them.

Preterists and idealists read these figures as real first-century teachers in Asia, and idealists also as types of compromise in every age. Some historicists and dispensational readers treat the seven churches as successive church ages, taking Pergamum as the church wedded to the state after Constantine and Thyatira as the medieval church, with Jezebel sometimes identified with corrupt Rome. Most futurists, while differing on the church ages, also read the letters as first addressed to real congregations.
Traditionally attributed to Moses; many scholars date its final form to the monarchy or the exile. It narrates creation to the patriarchs (Joseph in Egypt).

Genesis tells Israel's origin story against the backdrop of ancient Near Eastern creation and flood traditions from Mesopotamia and Egypt. It explains how a good creation was marred by human rebellion and how God chose Abraham's family to bring blessing back to the nations.
Creation and the garden
Promise of a victorious seed
Covenant with Noah and Abraham
Judgment on Babel and Sodom

Revelation never formally quotes the Old Testament with a citation formula, yet scholars agree it alludes to it constantly; estimates of the number of allusions vary widely depending on how strictly an allusion is defined. Genesis supplies the book's frame: what was lost in Genesis 1 to 3 (the tree of life, the river, God's presence, freedom from curse) is restored in Revelation 21 to 22, so the Bible's first and last pages mirror each other. The ancient serpent of Eden reappears as the dragon of Revelation 12, and the promise that the woman's seed would crush the serpent is played out as cosmic conflict. Readers of every school recognise this new-creation bookend, though they differ on whether it describes a renewed physical earth, a heavenly reality already present, or both.
Tree of life

Barred to humanity after the fall, the tree of life now stands on both banks of the river, bearing fruit monthly, with leaves for the healing of the nations. Revelation 2:7 already promises it to the one who conquers.
River of paradise
Eden's river that watered the garden becomes the river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb. Ezekiel 47 stands between the two texts.
Ancient serpent

The crafty serpent of Eden is explicitly identified as the great dragon, the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world. Genesis never names the serpent as Satan; Revelation makes the identification plain.
Woman, seed and enmity

Enmity between the serpent and the woman and her offspring becomes the dragon's war on the woman and 'the rest of her offspring', those who keep God's commandments. The child of Revelation 12:5 is widely read as the promised seed.
Curse removed
The ground cursed because of Adam is answered by 'no longer will there be anything accursed'. Zechariah 14:11 is also echoed here.
Rainbow

The bow set in the clouds as a sign of God's covenant not to destroy the earth by flood encircles God's throne, combined with Ezekiel 1:28. Many read it as a sign that judgment proceeds from a covenant-keeping God.
Fire, sulphur and rising smoke

The fire and sulphur that fell on Sodom and the smoke rising like a furnace become a pattern for judgment on those who worship the beast and on Babylon (Revelation 19:3). Revelation 11:8 also calls the great city 'Sodom' symbolically.
Sun, moon and twelve stars

Joseph's dream of sun, moon and eleven stars bowing to him (the twelfth star) lies behind the woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet, and a crown of twelve stars, linking her with Israel. Interpreters differ on whether she represents Israel, the church, Mary, or the people of God across both covenants.
Lion of the tribe of Judah
Jacob's blessing of Judah as a lion's cub who keeps the sceptre is announced in heaven, but John turns and sees a slain Lamb. The royal lion is redefined by the sacrificial lamb.
Traditionally attributed to Moses; describes Israel's deliverance from Egypt and covenant at Sinai, variously dated to the 15th or 13th century BC.

Exodus tells of Israel enslaved under a powerful Pharaoh, delivered by ten plagues, the Passover and the crossing of the sea. At Sinai God makes Israel a covenant people and comes to dwell among them in the tabernacle.
Plagues on an oppressive empire
Song of deliverance at the sea
Kingdom of priests
God dwelling in the tabernacle
The divine name 'I am'

Exodus is one of Revelation's deepest patterns: the church is pictured as a new Israel being brought out of a new Egypt. The trumpet and bowl judgments (Revelation 8 to 9 and 16) are modelled closely on the Egyptian plagues, the Lamb's blood redeems a people as the Passover blood did, and the redeemed sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb beside a sea. Sinai's thunder and lightning frame God's throne, and the people are made a kingdom and priests. Interpreters agree on the exodus pattern; they differ on whether the plagues describe literal future events, past judgments on Jerusalem or Rome, or recurring judgments throughout the church age.
The divine name
God's self-naming 'I am who I am' is expanded into 'him who is and who was and who is to come'. Greek translations of Exodus 3:14 render the name 'the one who is', which John adapts.
Water turned to blood
The first Egyptian plague returns in the second and third bowls and in the trumpets (Revelation 8:8-9). The two witnesses also have power to turn waters into blood (Revelation 11:6).
Painful sores
The boils that afflicted the Egyptians fall on those who bear the mark of the beast.
Hail and fire
Hail mixed with fire strikes the earth at the first trumpet, and enormous hailstones fall at the seventh bowl (Revelation 16:21).
Locusts
The eighth plague becomes demonic locusts from the abyss, now combined with Joel's locust army. The judgment is intensified but limited: they may not harm those sealed by God.
Darkness
Darkness over Egypt becomes darkness over the beast's kingdom; the fourth trumpet also darkens a third of the lights (Revelation 8:12).
Passover lamb
A lamb's blood once marked Israel's houses for protection; now a slain Lamb's blood ransoms people from every tribe and nation. The Lamb also echoes Isaiah 53:7.
Song of Moses at the sea

Israel sang beside the sea after Pharaoh's defeat; the conquerors stand beside a sea of glass mixed with fire and sing 'the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb'. Strikingly, the song celebrates the nations coming to worship God, not only their defeat.
Israel's calling at Sinai is applied to those freed by Christ's blood, from every nation (also Revelation 5:10 and 20:6).
Thunder, lightning and trumpet
The theophany at Sinai surrounds God's throne and recurs, growing more intense, at the close of the seals, trumpets and bowls (Revelation 8:5, 11:19, 16:18).
Traditionally attributed to Moses at Sinai; many scholars associate its final form with priestly circles of the later monarchy or exile.

Leviticus is a manual for worship and holiness in the tabernacle, addressed to a people camped at Sinai with a holy God in their midst. It governs sacrifice, priesthood, purity, the annual feasts and the covenant blessings and curses.
God dwelling among his people
Sacrifice and atonement
Priesthood and holiness
Feasts and the sacred calendar
Covenant blessings and sevenfold curses

Leviticus is used less visibly than the prophets, but it supplies much of the temple and priestly vocabulary that fills Revelation's heavenly scenes: altars, incense, blood, priestly garments and the hope of God dwelling among his people. Its covenant promise 'I will walk among you and be your God' is a key source for the climax in Revelation 21:3. Some commentators also see the sevenfold covenant curses of Leviticus 26 behind Revelation's series of seven judgments, though this is suggested rather than certain. A few links, such as the burning of a priest's unfaithful daughter, are pressed chiefly by interpreters who identify Babylon with first-century Jerusalem and are disputed by others.
God dwelling and walking among his people

The covenant promise that God would set his dwelling among Israel and be their God is fulfilled as 'the dwelling place of God is with man'. Revelation 2:1 also pictures Christ walking among the lampstands.
Sevenfold punishment

God warns four times that he will punish covenant breakers 'sevenfold'. Many commentators think this lies behind the structure of seven seals, trumpets and bowls; the link is thematic rather than verbal.
Censer, coals and incense

On the Day of Atonement the high priest took coals from the altar and incense before the Lord. An angel offers incense with the saints' prayers, then hurls the censer's fire to the earth as judgment (with Ezekiel 10:2).
Blood at the base of the altar
Sacrificial blood was poured out at the base of the altar; the souls of those slain for God's word are seen under the altar, portraying martyrdom as sacrifice.
Palm branches and booths
The Feast of Booths was celebrated with palm branches; the great multitude holds palm branches, and God will 'shelter them with his presence' (Revelation 7:15), using the verb for pitching a tent.
The priest's daughter burned

A priest's daughter who prostitutes herself is to be burned with fire; the harlot is burned (also Revelation 18:8). Interpreters who see Babylon as apostate Jerusalem stress this link, while those who see Babylon as Rome or a future world system regard it as background at most.
Composed over many centuries, from the time of David (c. 1000 BC) to after the exile, and collected for Israel's worship.

The Psalms are the prayer book and hymnal of Israel's temple and synagogue. They celebrate God as king over creation, voice laments under oppression, and hold up the hope of an anointed Davidic king who will rule the nations.
God enthroned as king
The anointed king and the raging nations
Laments asking 'How long?'
New songs of praise
The book of the living

Revelation's worship scenes are steeped in the Psalms, and its picture of Christ as king leans heavily on the royal psalms, above all Psalm 2. The nations rage against God and his anointed, and the Messiah rules them with a rod of iron, an image that appears three times in Revelation. The martyrs pray the lament 'How long?', heaven sings 'new songs', and the only New Testament uses of 'Hallelujah' occur in Revelation 19. Interpreters agree on these links but differ over when the Messiah's rule with the rod is exercised: now from heaven, at his return, or during a future earthly millennium.
Nations rage
The raging of nations against the Lord and his anointed is answered: 'the nations raged, but your wrath came'. Revelation 17:14 and 19:19 echo kings gathering against the Lamb.
Rod of iron

The Messiah 'will rule them with a rod of iron'. The phrase is applied to Christ (Revelation 12:5, 19:15) and promised to the one who conquers (Revelation 2:26-27), so the king's rule is shared with his people.
Firstborn and ruler of kings

God's promise to make David's heir 'the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth', alongside the moon as 'faithful witness in the skies' (89:37), stands behind Jesus as 'the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of kings on earth'.
A new song
The psalms call for a new song to the Lord (also 33:3, 98:1, 144:9). In Revelation the new song celebrates the Lamb's redemption (also 14:3).
How long, and avenge the blood
The psalm asks 'How long, O LORD?' and for the shed blood of God's servants to be avenged. The souls under the altar ask the same. They are told to rest a little longer.
All nations will come and worship
The song of Moses and the Lamb draws on the psalm's hope that all nations will come and worship before God, alongside echoes of Psalm 111:2 and 145:17 in Revelation 15:3.
Blotted out of the book
The psalmist prays that enemies be blotted out of the book of the living; Christ promises never to blot out the conqueror's name from the book of life.
Small and great who fear him
The Hallelujah psalms call the Lord's servants, 'both the small and the great', to praise. Revelation 19:1-6 is the only place in the New Testament that uses the Hebrew word Hallelujah.
Isaiah son of Amoz prophesied in Jerusalem c. 740 to 700 BC; many scholars assign chapters 40 to 66 to later prophets of the exile and return, while others defend single authorship.

Isaiah addresses Judah under the threat of Assyria and, in its later chapters, a people facing or returning from exile in Babylon. It sets the holy God of Israel against proud empires and promises a suffering servant, a restored Zion and new heavens and a new earth.
The holy one on his throne
The servant who suffers
Fall of Babylon
Day of the Lord and the winepress
Zion restored with gates open to the nations

Isaiah is probably the single most used prophet in Revelation by number of allusions, though some scholars give Ezekiel or Daniel greater structural weight. It supplies the thrice-holy throne vision, the titles 'first and last' and the key of David, the fall of Babylon and the harlot-queen's boast, and the warrior who treads the winepress. Above all, Revelation 21 to 22 is woven out of Isaiah 25, 54, 60 and 65: tears wiped away, a jewelled city, gates never shut, the nations walking by its light and new heavens and a new earth. The slain Lamb also recalls Isaiah's servant led like a lamb to the slaughter. Readers differ on whether the new creation describes a coming renewal of this world, a heavenly state, or a reality already begun in the church.
Isaiah's vision of the Lord enthroned with six-winged seraphim crying 'Holy, holy, holy' is merged with Ezekiel's living creatures, who sing it without ceasing.
First and the last
A title of the Lord alone (also 48:12), set against idols, is spoken by the risen Christ (also 2:8 and 22:13), a striking claim to share God's identity.
Key of David
The key given to the steward Eliakim, to open and none shall shut, belongs to Christ, who sets an open door before Philadelphia.
Lamb led to slaughter

The servant led like a lamb to slaughter stands behind the Lamb 'standing, as though it had been slain', combined with the Passover lamb. Revelation's word for lamb (arnion) differs from the Greek of Isaiah 53:7 (amnos), so the link is thematic.
Sky rolled up like a scroll

The host of heaven falling like leaves from a fig tree and the sky rolled up like a scroll describe the sixth seal. Preterists often read such language as stock prophetic imagery for the fall of a political order; futurists usually expect a cosmic event.
Fallen, fallen is Babylon

Isaiah's announcement of Babylon's fall (with Jeremiah 51:8) is repeated over the great city (also 14:8). Interpreters identify this Babylon with Rome, Jerusalem, a future world city or the world system in every age.
The queen's boast
Babylon's boast 'I shall not sit as a widow' and the sudden loss of children and widowhood in one day are applied to the harlot city, whose plagues come in a single day.
Treading the winepress

The warrior from Edom with garments stained from treading the winepress alone becomes the rider whose robe is dipped in blood. Many note that in Revelation the robe is bloodied before the battle, which some take as the Lamb's own blood.
